summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
Per GAO, twenty of 23 federal agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. Most reported use cases were in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported they were currently using AI. Reported uses included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. Some agencies also used AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate review of large datasets.

GAO found the inventories incomplete and inaccurate in many cases. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Two inventories included AI uses that were later determined by the agencies not to be AI. GAO also noted there is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and until all requirements are met, agencies cannot consistently manage AI risks and benefits. OMB has not yet developed acquisition and use guidance, OPM has not established or updated an occupational category for AI work, and OSTP did not communicate which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements.

Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to them, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Commerce and GSA fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing the AI Center of Excellence. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The excerpts do not identify vendor concentration or return on investment figures for government AI.

State legislative activity is substantial. The AI Laws tracker on theworldofai.org reports 5,926 AI bills tracked across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan. Per OECD.AI, the policy observatory gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, and in July 2024 the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand. OECD.AI also promotes the OECD AI Principles, which call for AI systems that are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe. Oxford Insights' Government AI Readiness Index scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, providing a standard cross-national comparison.

Stanford HAI's AI Index tracks government and policy through legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and it reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with governance frameworks falling behind and data transparency declining. For a reader deciding whether to deploy AI in government, GAO's audit shows the federal landscape is still early, with most use cases in planning, incomplete inventories, and missing acquisition guidance. State legislatures are active, and international policy infrastructure exists, but the sources do not provide ROI evidence, and a deployer should expect reporting and compliance requirements rather than proven returns.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: This source provides a state-by-state directory of artificial intelligence legislation in the United States, with links for all 50 states and the District of Columbia. It reports that 5,926 AI bills are tracked across 53 jurisdictions, with data updated daily from LegiScan. The page also lists books by Stephen R. Jordan, including the "Operating Discipline for AI Library" series, and several AI audit, governance, and security services.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
